fields.title: Svod: What Counts as Activation
fields.summary: Three departments offer three definitions. One is needed by Monday, and it will become the annual target.
fields.decisionPrompt: Which activation definition will you propose and why?
fields.brief/role: You are a product manager at Svod, responsible for metrics.
fields.brief/company: Svod is a fictional project management service for agencies: 21 400 registered companies in 14 months.
fields.brief/context: Leadership made activation the primary metric of the year: all team goals will tie back to it. There is no definition yet. Growth suggests "created a project," Account Management suggests "invited a colleague, who accepted," and Analytics suggests "completed three tasks in the first week." Each yields a different number and pulls the plan in its own direction. The CEO asks for one definition by Monday and promises to accept whichever one you can defend.
fields.brief/objective: Propose a single definition of activation and justify it.
fields.brief/constraints: Three days. Analytics can run queries, but will not add new tracking markup this week. The chosen option will become the company's target for four quarters.
fields.brief/task: Choose a definition and justify it.
fields.learnTakeaway/title: The primary metric is chosen using three checks, not correlation
fields.learnTakeaway/body: The strongest link to retention usually belongs to an event that simply happens more often for users who would stay anyway. You need to check: did moving the metric in the past actually move the result, does it work identically across segments, and what happens when people are incentivized to inflate it. A metric that is easy to boost without driving real impact turns a year of work into superficial reporting.
fields.evidenceCards/0/content:
Analytics calculated month-6 retention based on whether the event occurred in week 1. 14 months of signups, 21 400 companies.

Created a project: done by 68%. Retention is 24% for those who did, versus 6% for the rest.

Invited a colleague who accepted: done by 31%. Retention is 47% versus 11%.

Completed three tasks in week 1: done by 39%. Retention is 41% versus 9%.

Invited AND completed three tasks: done by 22%. Retention is 58%.

This is observational data, not an experiment: correlation may just mean these actions are taken by users who intended to stay regardless.
fields.evidenceCards/1/content:
Growth ran three tests over the year.

A prompt to create a project right during registration: project creation grew from 61% to 68%. Month-6 retention in this cohort is 23% versus 24%—no visible change.

Inviting a colleague after the first project: invitations grew from 24% to 31%. Retention grew from 19% to 22%—analytics calls this "a hint, not a conclusion."

A set of task templates: completing three tasks in a week grew from 33% to 39%, retention grew from 20% to 26%.

So all three can be moved, but the link to retention does not hold for all of them.
fields.evidenceCards/2/content:
From a session where the team asked themselves: if this becomes the shared target, how will people game it?

Created a project: Sales could create a project for the client during a demo. Already happening. Cheap to game, hard to spot.

Invited a colleague: On onboarding calls, rep can push hard for invites. The risk is that invitees won't return—the metric goes up, but people get annoyed. Partially visible via invitee return rate in week 2.

Completed three tasks: Hardest to game because tasks must actually be closed in the user's account; visible via mass creation of tasks with empty titles.

Team bonuses will be tied to the chosen number.
fields.evidenceCards/3/content:
Signups are divided into solo freelancers (34%), small studios of 2–9 people (49%), and agencies of 10+ people (17%).

Invited a colleague who accepted: freelancers 4%, studios 38%, agencies 71%.

Completed three tasks: freelancers 41%, studios 38%, agencies 39%.

Created a project: freelancers 66%, studios 68%, agencies 72%.

Revenue: freelancers 9%, studios 44%, agencies 47%.

Month-6 retention: freelancers 14%, studios 27%, agencies 39%.
fields.decisionOptions/0/label: Completed three tasks in the first week
fields.decisionOptions/0/description: A behavioral indicator of real usage: retention is 41% vs. 9%, the rate is nearly identical across all segments, and it is the hardest to game.
fields.decisionOptions/0/consequence:
The definition is accepted. It works equally well for freelancers, studios, and agencies—41%, 38%, and 39%—meaning teams working with freelancers are not set up to fail.
Growth tests show that the metric is moveable and the retention link holds: task templates raised the rate from 33% to 39%, and retention from 20% to 26%. Of the three candidates, this is the only one where moving the metric was accompanied by moving retention.
Attempts to game it run into the fact that tasks must be closed in the user's account; just in case, you ask analytics to check the share of tasks with blank titles once a month.
Drawback: retention among those who invited colleagues is higher (47%), and you have to explain to Account Management why their metric didn't become the goal—you answer with the segment breakdown.
Trade-off: you chose not the strongest correlation, but the most honest and universally applicable metric.
fields.decisionOptions/1/description: The strongest link to retention—47% vs. 11%—and Account Management knows how to influence it directly.
fields.decisionOptions/1/consequence:
The number looks like the best option, and that is its main trap: people invite colleagues when they have colleagues to invite. For freelancers, this rate is 4%, yet they make up a third of all signups.
Over the year, the team working with the small segment gets an unachievable target and gradually stops servicing them.
Onboarding managers push hard for invites; the rate goes up, but some invitees never return in week 2—the metric looks pretty, but brings no value.
By Q4, it turns out the metric grew by 40%, while retention barely moved.
Trade-off: you picked the strongest correlation, which actually reflects company size rather than product engagement.
fields.decisionOptions/2/description: The strongest link of all—58%. Activation as a high bar rather than a single event.
fields.decisionOptions/2/consequence:
The high bar indeed filters for users who stay: 58% at month 6.
However, only 22% of signups count as activated, almost all of them agencies with 10+ people. Freelancers and half the studios are excluded from the target by definition.
Furthermore, a composite metric is hard to interpret: when it stalls, it is unclear which part dipped, forcing teams to look at the individual components anyway.
Over the year, the metric grows from 22% to 26%, and no one can pinpoint why.
Trade-off: you chose the strongest correlation at the cost of losing an actionable and universal metric.
fields.decisionOptions/3/description: The simplest definition, clear to everyone, with the highest baseline—68%.
fields.decisionOptions/3/consequence:
The definition is accepted in an hour, ending the debate, which is its only merit.
Growth testing already revealed the core issue: the prompt raised project creation from 61% to 68%, but retention didn't budge at all—23% vs. 24%. In other words, moving the metric is easy, but yields no results.
Sales continues creating projects on behalf of clients during demos, and now they have an incentive to do it more often.
A year later, activation is 79%, while retention remains unchanged.
Trade-off: you chose what is easiest to measure and game, turning the annual goal into vanity reporting.
fields.rubric/remediation/0/gap: Research is not tied to the decision or the available choices
fields.rubric/remediation/1/gap: Metrics are listed flatly without separating primary, explanatory, and guardrail metrics
